paper.title: Have we lost sleep? A reconsideration of segmented sleep in early modern England

declarations.competing_interests: Not stated in the converted text.

definitions.definition: Ekirch's thesis that people in pre-industrial western Europe routinely slept in two segments, a 'first' and a 'second' sleep separated by up to an hour or more of wakefulness, and that consolidated sleep is a modern artefact of artificial light.
England in the sixteenth to eighteenth centuries, from which much of the thesis's textual evidence comes.

The printed and manuscript passages quoted by Ekirch as references to first and second sleep: Bentley (1582), Taillepied, Erasmus (1535), Bayly, Davenant, Baldwin, Fidge, Gombauld, Shirley, Amyraut and others.
A study of 16 participants (15 men, one woman) aged 20 to 36, one week at 16 h light and 8 h dark then four weeks at 10 h light and 14 h dark, confined to a dark room in the dark period.
Full-text searches of Early English Books Online for 'first sleep' and 'second sleep' in English printed texts of 1475-1700, each hit read in context.
Re-reading each quoted passage with its surrounding text, genre and circumstances of writing (illness, watch duty, prayer collections, figures of speech).
The early modern phrase whose meaning is at issue: a separate first segment of sleep, or the first, deepest or earliest part of a night's sleep, or an allocated watch.
Waking at night described as troublesome, caused by illness, fear, duty or circumstance, rather than as a routine interval.

claims.statement: Most passages of [[D3:Ekirch's textual sources]] describe [[D8:unusual or unwanted waking]] rather than a routine interval between two sleeps in [[D2:early modern England]].

relations.note: Ekirch reads these passages as evidence that segmented sleep was routine.

claims.statement: In [[D2:early modern England]] the phrase [[D7:first sleep]] carried several meanings, including the first or deepest part of a continuous night's sleep and an allocated watch, so its occurrence does not show segmented sleep.

[[D4:Wehr's photoperiod experiment]] does not support the [[D1:segmented sleep thesis]] for [[D2:early modern England]], because its participants lay in darkness without the candle and firelight of early modern evenings and its bimodal pattern was not quantified.

evidence.description: Re-reading in context of the passages Ekirch quotes as references to first and second sleep.

value.text: A prayer for waking at midnight, framed as troublesome and sent by God.
Written while ill with gout, so not a record of ordinary sleep.
The sleeper wakes from a frightening dream.

availability.comment: The sources are printed books in EEBO and other public collections.

evidence.description: Full-text EEBO searches for 'first sleep' (many hits, not counted) and 'second sleep' (15 hits), each read in context.

results.variable: EEBO hits naming both first and second sleep

value.text: the first sleepe is the deepe sleepe

availability.comment: EEBO, by subscription; the search terms are given.

warrants.text: A passage shows routine segmentation only if it presents night waking as ordinary; passages written in illness, about watches, in emergency prayers or as figures of speech present it as exceptional.

'First' commonly meant initial or earliest; used of sleep it can name the first, deepest part of one sleep, as in Caryl, as readily as a separate segment, and only 5 of 15 'second sleep' hits name both.
An experiment informs a historical claim only as far as its conditions resemble the historical ones; 14 hours confined in darkness do not resemble evenings lit by candle and fire.

limitations.statement: The author states that any alternative model of early modern sleep is by nature limited and uncertain, and does not deny that segmented sleep existed.
Hits for 'first sleep' were not counted, and EEBO covers printed English texts only, not manuscripts or speech.

references.target: Wehr TA. In short photoperiods, human sleep is biphasic. J Sleep Res 1992;1:103-107.
